summary: Marswalk Planner is a layered map of Gale Crater, NASA Curiosity's field site, that helps an astronaut plan a safe, science-rich Marswalk. It combines several NASA missions (MRO CTX imagery, MRO HiRISE 1 m slopes, MGS MOLA topography, CRISM/OMEGA minerals, Curiosity's real traverse) with an AI we trained on NASA/JPL's labelled Curiosity photos to spot sand and big rocks. Click a route and get distance, climb, slope risk, sand/rock risk, science stops and walking time. On NASA's official test set the AI catches 96% of the sand (mIoU 0.777 vs 0.056 baseline).
details: Marswalk Planner is a layered, interactive map of Gale Crater (NASA Curiosity's field site) that helps an astronaut plan a safe, science-rich Marswalk. It has three parts: 1) Marswalk Map: combines data from several NASA missions in one view: MRO CTX satellite imagery, MRO HiRISE 1 m elevation for slope hazards (orange >15°, red >25°), MGS MOLA topography outside HiRISE coverage, CRISM/OMEGA water-related mineral signals, and Curiosity's real traverse and science stops. The user clicks waypoints and gets a route report: distance, walk time, slope risk, share of route on steep ground, AI sand/big-rock risk from nearby rover photos, share on Curiosity's proven path, climb/descent, max slope, an elevation profile and a per-leg table showing which elevation data was used. 2) AI ground checks: 319 real Curiosity Navcam photos analysed by our AI and pinned to the exact spot they were taken. Each NASA filename carries the rover's site/drive code, which we match to NASA MMGIS waypoints (287 exact, 32 interpolated). 3) AI Ground Check tab: upload or pick a rover photo; the model maps soil, bedrock, sand and big rocks and draws the safest path through it with a GO / CAUTION / HOLD verdict. How the AI works: Meta's DINOv2-small vision model (frozen) describes each part of the image, and a LightGBM classifier we trained on 1,500 labelled NASA/JPL AI4Mars Curiosity images decides the terrain class. It runs on a normal laptop CPU in about 2 seconds per image. Validation: on NASA's official AI4Mars expert test set (never seen in training), strictest split test_min3: mIoU 0.777 vs 0.056 for an always-"bedrock" baseline; sand recall 96.3%; pixel accuracy 97.8% (looser splits: mIoU 0.665 and 0.711). 16/16 automated tests pass. WHAT BENEFITS DOES IT HAVE? - Safety: shows steep slopes, sand traps and big rocks along a planned walk before the astronaut goes. - Science: highlights mineral signals and Curiosity's science stops near the route. - Trust: every number shows its source, and the app clearly says where only orbital data exists. - Practical: runs offline-capable on a normal laptop, with no GPU or cloud. WHAT IS THE INTENDED IMPACT? The first humans on Mars will be on their own: radio delay rules out real-time help from Earth. Soft sand ended NASA's Spirit rover in 2009, and steep slopes and big rocks are serious dangers for someone in a spacesuit carrying tools. Our goal is to turn NASA's existing orbital and rover data into a walk-level safety and science plan, and the same approach can support rover drive planning today. WHAT TOOLS, LANGUAGES, HARDWARE AND SOFTWARE DID YOU USE? Python, Gradio (web app), Leaflet (interactive map), PyTorch, Meta DINOv2-small, LightGBM, scikit-learn, NumPy, Hugging Face datasets, pytest, Git/GitHub, Vercel (web version). Data from NASA Mars Trek, NASA MMGIS and NASA/JPL AI4Mars. Developed and run on a standard laptop CPU. HOW IS YOUR PROJECT CREATIVE? Instead of only displaying rover photos, we trained an AI on them and placed its findings on the map at the exact locations they were taken, next to orbital slope and mineral layers. Hidden location codes in NASA's own filenames let us geolocate the photos precisely. We also tested an unfamiliar-terrain check that flagged held-out big rocks with AUROC 0.964. WHAT FACTORS DID YOUR TEAM CONSIDER? - Astronaut safety first, as NASA's challenge asks: slopes, sand, big rocks, unknown ground. - Honesty about limits: big rocks are rare (0.1–0.2% of pixels) and over-predicted, which makes routes more cautious; ground photos exist only where Curiosity drove; HiRISE 1 m slope covers part of Gale and MOLA is used elsewhere (labelled per leg); our unfamiliar-terrain check did not separate Perseverance's Jezero images from Curiosity's; JPL's published results (DeepLabv3 >96% accuracy, SPOCv2 91.41%) used a different setup and are shown as reference only. - Running without special hardware, since there is no cloud on Mars. - Next steps: nearest real rover photo per route leg ("what you'll see"), helmet-camera live ground check, route modes (safest, fastest, science-rich, emergency return when low on oxygen), suit time and return-to-base, and radiation dose per walk.
